title: Ghostly Halos Revealed: MIT Scientists Map the Universe's Missing Matter
summary: For decades, a cosmic accounting puzzle has stumped astrophysicists: the universe contains only about a tenth of the ordinary, baryonic matter that should exist based on early-universe measurements. Where is the rest? Now, an MIT-led team using the Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME) has pinpointed it—in vast, diffuse halos around galaxies. The key is fast radio bursts (FRBs), millisecond flashes of radio waves from distant, energetic sources. As an FRB travels through space, free electrons in intervening matter cause lower frequencies to lag, "smearing" the signal. This dispersion measure is directly proportional to the amount of matter along the line of sight. By cross-correlating dispersion measures of thousands of CHIME-detected FRBs with the locations of millions of galaxies from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) survey, the researchers isolated the signal of missing matter. They found that the gas extends far beyond the visible galaxy, forming halos on scales much larger than predicted. "We're not just probing if the gas is with the galaxy or not, but we are seeing the shape of the missing matter that's around the galaxies," said Haochen Wang, an MIT graduate student and lead author of the study published in Physical Review Letters. The results indicate that feedback processes—jets from supermassive black holes and supernova explosions—are more powerful than models suggest, ejecting matter to greater distances. This baryonic matter exists at extremely low densities, around one proton per cubic meter, making it nearly impossible to detect directly. FRBs, however, act as cosmic lighthouses, illuminating this hidden reservoir. The findings not only resolve the missing baryon problem but also provide a new tool for mapping the large-scale structure of the universe. As CHIME continues to detect thousands more FRBs, astronomers will refine this map, revealing how galaxies interact with their environments over cosmic time. The ghostly halos are no longer missing—they are the faint, pervasive fabric connecting the cosmos.
why_it_matters: Understanding how invisible forces and matter shape galaxies and the universe helps us see that science is a detective story, and new tools can solve old mysteries—inspiring careers in astronomy, physics, and data analysis that shape how we view our place in the cosmos.

background_read: Astrophysicists have long known that about 5% of the universe's energy density is ordinary (baryonic) matter, but when they counted up stars and gas in galaxies, they could only find about half of it—the 'missing baryon problem'.

The Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME, a radio telescope in British Columbia) was originally designed to map hydrogen, but its ability to detect fast radio bursts has made it a crucial tool for cosmic accounting.

Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are millisecond flashes of radio energy originating far beyond the Milky Way; their signal is dispersed by any electrons they pass through, so measuring that dispersion reveals the amount of intervening matter.
The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI, a massive galaxy survey mapping millions of galaxies) provided the galaxy positions needed to correlate with the FRB signals.

By combining CHIME data with DESI maps, the MIT team showed that the missing matter lies in enormous, tenuous halos around galaxies, pushed outward by feedback from black holes and supernovae—a discovery that solves a decades-old puzzle.

perspectives.description: For astronomers, this is a major vindication of simulations that predicted gas halos, and it opens a new way to study galaxy environments using fast radio bursts as natural probes.

Some researchers caution that the statistical correlations may be affected by unknowns in FRB host galaxy identification, and the exact nature of the feedback mechanisms remains unclear because the gas is too thin to observe in other ways.

The method elegantly turns transient cosmic events into searchlights, and it shows how combining data from radio astronomy and optical galaxy surveys can answer fundamental questions that neither could solve alone—a template for future discovery.

As CHIME detects tens of thousands more FRBs, astronomers will be able to create three-dimensional maps of the cosmic web, potentially revealing how galaxies exchange matter and how the large-scale structure of the universe evolved.
